$$
\begin{aligned}
&\oint_C\left(ye^{xy}+y^2\right)\,\mathrm{d}x
+\left(xe^{xy}+x^2y\right)\,\mathrm{d}y\\
&\qquad=\iint_D f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}A.
\end{aligned}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The ordered vertices trace the left side upward, the top side to the right, the right side downward and the bottom side to the left. The interior stays on the traveler's right, so $C$ is clockwise.

![The shaded unit square with arrows pointing clockwise.](images/91/91aadfb7b45c720c35a0aca6158d87f5e5eae700f9537f259015236df3359c7e.png)

Reversing a curve reverses the sign of its line integral. Thus the clockwise version of Green's theorem is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\oint_C P\,\mathrm{d}x+Q\,\mathrm{d}y
&=-\iint_D(Q_x-P_y)\,\mathrm{d}A\\
&=\iint_D(P_y-Q_x)\,\mathrm{d}A.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $P=ye^{xy}+y^2$ and $Q=xe^{xy}+x^2y$. Both functions have continuous first partial derivatives throughout the plane. Apply the product and chain rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P_y&=e^{xy}+xy e^{xy}+2y,\\
Q_x&=e^{xy}+xy e^{xy}+2xy.
\end{aligned}
$$

Now use the order of subtraction appropriate to this clockwise traversal:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x,y)&=P_y-Q_x\\
&=\left(e^{xy}+xy e^{xy}+2y\right)
-\left(e^{xy}+xy e^{xy}+2xy\right)\\
&=2y-2xy\\
&=2y(1-x).
\end{aligned}
$$

Both exponential terms cancel. Using $Q_x-P_y$ without correcting the orientation would instead give $2xy-2y$, the negative of the required integrand.
